289: If he made it like a bolt, it is invalid.  In chapter HaKometz, there is a statement of Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav.  The Gemara challenges this:  "But when Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yosef came, he said: 'All the mezuzot of Rabbi's house were made like a bolt.'"  The Gemara answers:  "There is no difficulty. One was made like a peg, and the other was made like an istivra."  Rashi explains:  "Made it like a bolt" means that he fixed it and inserted it into the doorpost like a bolt that carpenters insert into a wall. It is invalid because the mitzvah is to place it lengthwise in the doorpost.  "Nagar" means a bolt.  "Istivra" means the place where the shin and foot are joined, and it is upright; therefore it is valid.  "Made like a peg" means like a craftsman's peg, and it is invalid.  Rashi gives another explanation:  Just as at the junction of the shin and foot, the shin stands upright above and the foot lies horizontally, so too if he placed the mezuzah in this manner, it is valid, since one of its ends is upright.  Tosafot and the Rosh write that Rabbenu Tam objected to Rashi's explanation, because an upright position is not honorable. In Bava Batra it is called a "donkey burial." The Torah scroll and the Tablets in the Ark were lying down and not standing upright.  One can also learn from common practice: when the Torah scroll is standing, all the congregation stands; when the prayer leader lays it down, everyone sits.  Therefore Rabbenu Tam explained that "like a peg" means upright, like the stakes of the Tabernacle fixed in the ground, and this is invalid. "Like an istivra" means laid across the width of the leg (called cabille in Old French), and this is valid.  However, in tractate Yevamot, where it says, "This istivra extends down to the ground," it must refer to the bone descending from the shin to the foot and not to a cabille.  Regarding the statement in the Jerusalem Talmud that the word "Shema" must face the entrance:  According to Rashi, when he rolls the parchment toward the word "Shema," he positions it so that "Shema" faces the airspace of the doorway and not the interior.  According to Rabbenu Tam, he turns the last line toward the public domain and the first line toward the interior, so that the line containing "Shema" faces the doorway.  The Rosh writes that nowadays the accepted practice follows Rashi.  The Mordechai also writes this and says that this is the primary ruling, bringing proof for it.  Tosafot and the Rosh further note that the statement "All the mezuzot in Rabbi's house were made like a bolt" implies that ordinary mezuzot were not made this way. Yet certainly neither Rabbi's mezuzot nor everyone else's were invalid.  Therefore it appears that the valid form called istivra is diagonal—neither horizontal nor vertical. Alternatively, it resembles a bent Hebrew letter nun, partly horizontal and partly upright.  Rashi also explained it this way in his alternative interpretation.  Ordinary mezuzot were not made this way. Rather, according to Rashi they were upright, and according to Rabbenu Tam they were horizontal.  The Rosh writes that the mezuzot of Maharam were shaped like a bent letter nun.  The Mordechai writes that the Bahag explained istivra as half upright and half horizontal, while the Ri explained it as slanted, because with a mezuzah it is impossible for part of it literally to be upright and part horizontal.  Rabbeinu Yerucham writes that some explain it as diagonal—neither upright nor horizontal, but slightly inclined, with the lower end of the mezuzah somewhat away from the wall. He adds, "So I saw my teachers practice."  He further writes that the general custom followed Rashi and placed the mezuzah upright. Others explain istivra as a bent nun, half horizontal and half upright, and this was the practice of Maharam.  The Rambam's view follows Rashi. He writes in chapter 5 that if one hollowed out the doorpost and inserted the mezuzah like a bolt, like the bar that passes through the rings of boards, it is invalid.
